questions.q: In $f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}$, what is the job of the factor $\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$?
options: It shifts the curve left or right
It normalizes the curve so the total area equals exactly 1
questions.explain: Without the normalizer the area under the bell would not be 1, so it would not be a valid probability distribution. Symmetry comes from squaring $(x-\mu)/\sigma$; the shift comes from $\mu$.

questions.q: You shrink $\sigma$ from $1.5$ to $0.2$ (keeping $\mu = 0$). What happens to the peak height $f(0)$?
options: It drops because the curve is thinner
It is capped at 1 because it is a probability
It rises from about $0.27$ to about $1.99$ — densities can exceed 1
questions.explain: $f(\mu) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$: $\approx 0.266$ at $\sigma = 1.5$ and $\approx 1.995$ at $\sigma = 0.2$. A thinner bell must get taller to keep area 1; a density value is not a probability.

questions.q: For a Normal distribution, about what fraction of values falls within $\mu \pm 2\sigma$?
questions.explain: The 68.3 / 95.4 / 99.7 rule covers $\pm 1, 2, 3\,\sigma$. Tails are never exactly zero, so it is never 100%.

questions.q: Which AI use of the Normal distribution is described on the page?
options: Softmax outputs are always Normally distributed
Neural network weights are initialized to exactly zero
Diffusion models start from pure Gaussian noise and gradually denoise it into an image
Decision trees split on the bell curve
questions.explain: Diffusion models (e.g. Stable Diffusion) denoise Gaussian static. Weights are *sampled* from a Normal (not set to zero) to break symmetry, and VAEs push their latent space toward a standard Normal.
